source.title: On the Robustness of Machine Unlearning for Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Yu-Jie Lin; Kaidi Jia; Jia-Yao Ma; Cheng-Yi Yang; Jinsong Su

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened or difficult to align, but Appendix Tables 7 and 8 provide aligned attack results.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests contextual prompting and retraining attacks on unlearned VLMs. Its results show recovery in some settings but not others, refining the claim that unlearning generally hides rather than removes knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper also surveys methods and gives initial evaluations under original, paraphrased, and discriminative prompts. Survey descriptions and cited results are not recorded as rows. Detailed InD/OOD tables report many method-by-proportion-by-prompt outcomes; only key contrasts and explicitly summarized findings are included. The flattened Table 2 is not used for numerical in-context attack values.
record.test_reason: The study attacks 13 unlearned Qwen2.5-VL-3B models (VGGFace2 identity forgetting) in three ways: identity-related context prompts, in-distribution re-fine-tuning on 0–100% of the forget set, and OOD fine-tuning on PACS. It reports forgetting and retention scores for each, so it directly tests B and E, and A's 'simple attacks don't recover it', in a new setting (VLMs). None of its authors' papers are original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that many VLM unlearning methods hide rather than remove knowledge: context cues and InD retraining reactivate it, while OOD retraining mainly harms retention. The record omits that the authors find vision-encoder methods (HFRU, HFRU-SFT) more robust, and Mmunlearner the most robust to InD retraining.
record.recipe_differences: This is a VLM robustness study using identity recognition on Qwen2.5-VL3B-Instruct. It tests contextual cues and further fine-tuning on in-distribution and OOD data; it does not reproduce text-only LLM unlearning experiments or test weight quantization or activation ablation.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack outcomes vary by unlearning method, retraining-data proportion, and prompt type. Mmunlearner is more robust under InD retraining; discriminative prompts show no clear InD trend; OOD retraining trends oppositely to recovery.
record.problems: The authors note that some implementation details were simplified and contextual prompts were manually constructed. The in-context attack values in Table 2 are difficult to align in the flattened text; the paper provides many attack-sweep results, but no uncertainty estimates are stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: The complete InD and OOD tables contain separate results across 13 methods, multiple proportions or sample counts, three prompt types, and forget/retain splits. Those exhaustive combinations are omitted under the 60-row cap; selected rows and the authors' explicit aggregate descriptions capture the key recovery, robustness, and non-recovery contrasts. General-benchmark utility values and flattened Table 2 entries were not assigned because the supplied layout does not support reliable method-to-value alignment.

untested.parts: Text-only LLMs; hazardous-knowledge benchmarks such as WMDP; chance-level accuracy measured as multiple-choice accuracy.
Loosely related (as opposed to unrelated) relearning data; a comparison with learning the facts from scratch at the same data budget.
Not tested: no activation-direction ablation and no internal-mechanism analysis. The discriminative-probe gap is behavioural only.
Jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context provision of the forgotten facts themselves.
Not tested: no new robust method is proposed.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3 (new VLM setting, single 3B model, 3 forget identities, no uncertainty estimates). Several methods (SatImp, WGA, RMU) barely forget initially, and GA/GD/NPO/SimNPO/UNDIAL forget by collapsing retention. These must be excluded when reading attack resistance as evidence of real removal. InD labels come from the original model, so InD relearning is effectively re-teaching the facts. There is no control that trains a never-exposed model to the same budget.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests VLMs, not text-only LLMs, and does not test activation ablation or quantization. It does not establish whether every method brings targeted accuracy to chance while preserving general ability.

In-distribution retraining uses samples from the forget distribution with labels generated by the original model. The OOD dataset is described as unrelated to the VGGFace2 identities. Other kinds of loosely related examples are not tested.

No activation-direction ablation or internal editing experiment is performed. The authors discuss residual associations as an interpretation of attack results, not as a direct internal-mechanism test.
The study tests manually constructed contextual cues and evaluates paraphrased prompts, but does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context demonstrations that supply forgotten facts.
No newer counter-method is proposed and tested for resistance to the attacks.

rows.value: Authors report that full-parameter methods generally achieve strong forgetting on original and paraphrased prompts, but many substantially damage retention and general utility.
rows.note: Qualitative summary; it does not show that all methods preserve general ability while reaching near-chance target accuracy.

statements.correction: HFRU = Jia, Lin, Yang, Ma, Su 2026, arXiv:2605.08031: same five authors as 2605.26992. In 2605.26992 (Qwen2.5-VL-3B only), HFRU For. is 99.67 original, 99.67 paraphrased, 96.00 discriminative and 99.67 in-context, with utility 60.47 vs vanilla 59.92. InD retraining cuts HFRU original For. to 3.33 at 25%.
statements.problem: The 'why' says the headers don't say whether 2605.26992's authors overlap with HFRU's. The reference list shows HFRU (arXiv:2605.08031) is by the same five authors, so the study's HFRU results are not independent. In this study HFRU's discriminative For. is 96.00, and InD retraining does undo HFRU (3.33 at 25%).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: In-context attacks on the tested VGGFace2 unlearning methods
reader_labels.reason: Contextual cues partially reactivate forgotten knowledge; RAZOR and SLUG are specifically reported as successfully attacked, so attacks do recover knowledge in tested settings (r2–r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The authors report strong forgetting on generative prompts for many methods but substantial losses in retention and general utility, so the joint forgetting-and-utility condition is not consistently met (r1).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: In-distribution retraining, especially SLUG and other less robust methods
reader_labels.reason: Forgetting scores fall sharply after forget-distribution fine-tuning; SLUG shows a large decline at 1%, and the authors report recovery for most methods on generative prompts (r6,r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Mmunlearner is reported as the most robust method, with significant degradation occurring only after 50% or 75% retraining depending on prompt type; the effect depends on method and data amount (r7,r8,r10).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Forgetting performance improved rather than deteriorated across prompt settings as OOD data increased, contrary to the expected recovery (r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The attack has no clear or consistent effect on forgetting performance in this prompt setting (r12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Indirect contextual cues in the in-context attack
reader_labels.reason: The study reports partial reactivation across paradigms and successful attacks on RAZOR and SLUG using contextual cues (r2–r5).
